rationale: The plasma samples were run in two acquisition batches, and batch shifts in DIA intensities per protein can hide the AD signal or be mistaken for it. This change centres each protein on its median within each batch, using only quantified values. That step uses no labels and is done in `featurize`. Everything else stays the same, so any change in score comes from batch harmonization alone.

Low-abundance proteins that leak from the brain or reflect inflammation are often quantified in only some plasma samples. In DIA, whether a protein is quantified depends on its abundance, so the missing pattern itself carries signal. I am lowering the quantification filter from 70% to 50% of training samples, so these proteins come in with half-minimum imputation, which encodes both their level and whether they were detected. The strong L2 penalty stays the same to keep the extra features from overfitting.

With DIA, low-abundance proteins drop out depending on abundance. So a sample's median over its observed proteins shifts with how deep that run went: samples that quantify more low-abundance proteins get a lower median, and every protein in them is pushed up. I am computing the per-sample normalization median only over a fixed reference set of proteins quantified in nearly every sample (at least 95%). That keeps depth differences from leaking into all features, and everything else stays the same.

Plasma MS profiles often carry contamination from sample handling: lysed red blood cells (haemoglobin, CA1, PRDX2…) and activated platelets (PF4, PPBP, ITGA2B, TLN1…). This pre-analytical variation can swamp a small AD signal when n is about 89. Inside `featurize`, and without using labels, I build per-sample erythrocyte and platelet contamination indices from these marker panels. I then regress the indices out of every protein (observed values only) and drop the marker proteins themselves. Everything else stays the same.

Plasma DIA data contain many immunoglobulin protein groups (IGHV/IGKV/IGLV variable regions, IGHG/IGKC/IGLC constant chains, JCHAIN). Their levels mostly reflect each person's antibody repertoire and humoral state, not AD, and they are strongly correlated with each other. Under the L2 penalty these noisy groups can take a large share of the model's weight together. This change drops them in `featurize`, using gene names only (no labels). Normalization, harmonization and the model stay the same, so any change in score comes from removing them.

Plasma proteomes contain sporadic extreme values, such as acute-phase spikes in single people and the far tail created by half-minimum imputation. After standardization these can reach z-scores of 5 or more, and a few samples then dominate the L2 logistic regression weights when n is about 71 per training fold. I clip the standardized features to ±3, with the scaler fitted on the training fold only, to limit that leverage without discarding any proteins. The rest of the pipeline is unchanged, so any change in score comes from clipping alone.

L2-LR currently uses a fixed C=0.05, but the right amount of shrinkage depends on how many proteins pass the filter and how strong the signal is in each training fold. With ~71 samples, I choose C by grouped inner CV on the training fold only. Preprocessing is redone inside each inner fold, and when scores are close I pick the stronger-regularized model so the choice doesn't overfit.

I'm multiplying the standardized values of a fixed, label-free panel of AD-related proteins by 2. This panel is the amyloid chaperones and transport proteins, the complement cascade, neuronal and glial leakage markers, and lipid transport proteins. Under L2 that cuts the effective penalty on them by 4×, so the model leans on established plasma AD biology instead of spreading weight over thousands of noisy proteins when n is about 71.

The two acquisition batches can differ in the spread of each protein's values (dynamic range, ion statistics), not just in their medians, and round 1 only fixed the medians. This round adds a label-free scale step like ComBat's: each protein's observed values are rescaled within each batch to the pooled within-batch SD. The log scale ratio is shrunk toward 1 when a batch has few observed values and is clipped, so small n cannot inflate noise. Everything else stays the same.

Low-abundance proteins that leak from the brain (GFAP, NEFL, YWHAG, SMOC1, NPTX2, CHI3L1, …) are often quantified in fewer than 70% of plasma samples, so the current filter drops them. Round 2 showed that relaxing the filter for every protein brings in too much noise. This change relaxes it only for the fixed, label-free prior AD panel (kept if quantified in ≥30% of training samples). Half-minimum imputation then records both their level and their abundance-dependent detection, while the rest of the proteome keeps the strict 70% filter.

Individual prior-panel proteins are noisy when n is about 71 per fold. This change adds four module scores built from the fixed AD prior groups: amyloid chaperones and transport, complement cascade, neuronal and glial injury, and lipid transport. Each score is the average of that group's standardized proteins, re-standardized on the training fold. They get the same reduced L2 penalty as the panel, so the model can use the module-level signal, which is more stable than any single protein.

Plasma AD proteomics studies repeatedly report a systemic inflammatory and acute-phase signature (SERPINA1, ITIH family, ORM1/2, HP/HPX, SAA, CRP, LRG1, fibrinogen, CP, AHSG, AGT). The project brief also points to inflammation in plasma, but the prior panel has no such module. These proteins are abundant and quantified in nearly every sample, so they are reliable at n≈71. This change adds them as a fifth fixed, label-free module, which gives them the same reduced penalty and a module score.

The L2 model spreads its weight over roughly 2,000 proteins, and with about 71 training samples per fold most of them are probably noise that dilutes the AD signal. This change keeps the fixed prior panel and the module scores, and adds only the 300 non-prior proteins with the largest Welch |t|, ranked on the training fold only. Everything else stays the same, so any change in score comes from this pre-filter.

Some prior-panel markers behave in threshold-like, non-additive ways. Plasma ApoE level is mostly set by APOE genotype (ε4 carriers have lower levels), and neuroglial leakage markers only rise past a certain point, so the L2-LR can only fit these linearly. I am averaging its probability with an ExtraTrees model (strongly regularized, fixed seed) trained only on the roughly 60 prior-panel proteins plus the module scores. This adds a low-variance, biology-restricted nonlinear view without opening the trees up to thousands of noisy proteins.

Low-abundance brain-derived prior markers (GFAP, NEFL, YWHAG, SMOC1, NPTX2, CHI3L1…) are often detected in fewer than 70% of plasma samples, so the current filter drops them. Round 10 brought them back for the linear model and saw no gain, because a linear model can't use a detection threshold well. A tree split on a half-minimum-imputed feature can: it separates "detected and high" from "below detection". So the ExtraTrees view, and only that view, now gets prior-panel proteins quantified in at least 30% of training samples. The L2-LR and its inputs stay exactly as they are.

Some plasma prior markers are better read relative to their biological carrier or module than as absolute levels. Plasma ApoE, for example, depends on both genotype and how much lipoprotein is circulating, and complement proteins rise together during systemic activation. A linear model can form these differences itself, but axis-aligned ExtraTrees splits cannot. This change adds within-module contrast features (protein z-score minus its module mean, i.e. log-ratios to the module) to the ExtraTrees view only. The L2-LR stays exactly as it was.

I'm adding the top 5 principal components of the whole filtered proteome to the ExtraTrees view only. They are fitted without labels on the training fold and then projected onto the test fold. They give the trees a summary of each person's overall plasma state (lipoprotein, acute-phase or liver-synthesis axes), so a split on a prior AD marker can depend on that context. The L2-LR stays exactly as it is.

The round-16 contrasts compare ApoE and clusterin with their own amyloid module, not with the lipoproteins that carry them, even though the docstring claims otherwise. Plasma ApoE and CLU sit mostly on HDL/VLDL, and APOE ε4 carriers have less ApoE per lipoprotein particle. So this change adds, to the ExtraTrees view only, each amyloid-module protein relative to the lipid-transport module mean (a carrier-normalized log-ratio). The L2-LR stays exactly as it is.

With half-minimum imputation, a protein quantified in only 70–90% of training samples has a block of identical values 1 log2 unit below its minimum. After standardization, much of its variance comes from that detection/imputation pattern rather than from measured abundance, yet the L2-LR currently gives it the same prior weight as a protein measured in every sample. This change multiplies each protein's scale in the LR by its observed fraction on the training fold. That is a label-free, imputation-aware penalty: up to about 2× more shrinkage for the most heavily imputed proteins. The prior-panel up-weighting, module scores and the ExtraTrees view stay unchanged.

This round adds a fifth fixed, label-free prior module for vascular and blood-brain-barrier biology, because AD involves vascular and BBB damage that shows up in plasma. The module includes adhesion molecules VCAM1/ICAM1/SELE, endothelial proteins VWF/CDH5/PECAM1/THBD/PROCR and pericyte/angiogenic receptors PDGFRB/NOTCH3/TEK/KDR/ENG, all of which Astral DIA quantifies well. Its proteins get the reduced prior penalty and a module score in the LR. The ExtraTrees view gets the same proteins plus within-module contrasts. Round 12's acute-phase module, a different biology, was dropped; nothing else changes.
